summary: Mobility is returning to near‑normal levels (MF‑Index 71) while fuel prices remain high, limiting any spontaneous shift to public transport. Public‑transport ridership is still about 13% below pre‑pandemic daily levels, and actual fuel savings from the work‑from‑home mandate are negligible, highlighting gaps in policy effectiveness.

signals.detail: The theoretical ceiling of 35.7 M L/week saved is far from reality; only 334 k L were recorded in the first week, roughly 1% of the modelled target, indicating the WFH mandate is not delivering meaningful fuel reductions.
Daily PT trips stand at 1.24 M, about 13% below the 2019 baseline of ~1.43 M, but the ridership component of the MF‑Index remains at 72.7, suggesting modest recovery without a clear upward trend.

High‑mobility sectors (Logistics, Construction, Retail) show mobility scores above 85 and are classified as HIGH risk, exposing the economy to congestion, emissions spikes, and supply‑chain disruptions as activity rebounds.
WFH adoption is uneven: 60% in Public & GLCs versus only 5–8% in Logistics, Construction and Retail, creating inequitable exposure to fuel costs and travel burdens across the workforce.

Elevated RON95 (RM4.32/L) and diesel (RM5.07/L) prices could incentivise a shift to mass transit, yet low actual fuel savings and persistent high private‑vehicle mobility in key sectors dampen the expected modal transition.

recommendation: Introduce sector‑targeted WFH incentives to raise remote work to at least 30% in Logistics, Construction and Retail by Q2 2027, coupled with a graduated congestion charge in high‑traffic corridors to curb private‑vehicle trips. Simultaneously, allocate RM1.2 bn to expand PT capacity and frequency to achieve a daily ridership of 1.4 M by end‑2027, and offer fuel‑efficiency rebates for fleets that adopt low‑emission vehicles.
